subtopic: TABLING OF ORDER IN COUNCIL SETTING FORTH FURTHER RESTRICTIONS

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: TABLING OF ORDER IN COUNCIL SETTING FORTH FURTHER RESTRICTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to table a copy of order in council P.C. 1249 dated March 13, 1951, and made under the authority of the Consumer Credit (Temporary Provisions) Act, 1950. The initial regulations made under this act were published late in October and became effective on November 1 last. The terms and conditions laid down by these regulations respecting minimum down payments and maximum periods of credit were generally more restrictive than prevailing business practice, but were not as severe as those which we had during the war, nor have they been as restrictive as the revised American regulations which became effective a few months ago.
As hon. members are aware, there have been discussions recently between the Bank of Canada and the chartered banks regarding the most effective means of restraining the inflationary expansion of bank credit. As a result of these discussions one of the steps the chartered banks have taken is- to call a halt to further expansion of loans on the security of instalment finance paper.
In conjunction with this move, and with the same purpose of restraining inflationary credit expansion, the consumer credit regulations have been amended by the order in council which I have just tabled. The new regulations will come into effect next Monday, March 19.
The principal changes being introduced are:
First, in the case of motor cars the minimum down payment is increased from one-third of the cash price to one-half of the cash price.
Second, in the case of all other commodities affected by the regulations the minimum down payment is increased from one-fifth to one-third of the cash price.
Third, in all cases the minimum down payment will be not less than $10 instead of $5 under the former regulations.
Fourth, the maximum period of credit has been reduced from eighteen months to twelve

months, and the minimum size of instalment payments has been increased to $10 a month or $2.50 a week, as compared with $5 a month or $1.25 a week under the previous regulations.
Fifth, under what is known in the trade as a revolving credit plan, the minimum initial down payment is increased to $10, and wherever new purchases are made under existing credits the minimum monthly instalment is increased to $10.
Finally, as a result of varied representations and a further review of the effects of the present regulations we have decided that the consumer credit restrictions should not apply to the sale of books.
In their net effect the new regulations will be much stiffer than those now in effect, but except in the case of motor cars they will be no stiffer, and in some cases not quite so stiff as those in effect during the war. During the war we required a one-third down payment for cars, and if the amount remaining to be financed exceeded $500 the purchaser had fifteen months in which to complete his payments. Now we are requiring fifty per cent down and the balance spread over twelve months. Hon. members will realize, of course, that where an old car is being turned in, its trade-in value will normally constitute the greater part if not the whole of the required down payment.
In the case of other commodities our new regulations require one-third down and the balance over twelve months. During the war the same down payment was required, but the balance had to be paid in ten months, unless the amount to be financed exceeded $500.

speechtext:
Yesterday, before the orders of the day were called, the member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) asked a question which I thought was one that should have been placed on the order paper. Upon reading the question in Hansard, it seems to

me there is some urgency in connection with the matter which he has raised. In view of the fact that today we are not likely to reach orders of the day, may I suggest that the hon. member for Vancouver East ask his question at this time.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO DECISION TO MOVE SEAT OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I had an idea that when you saw my question in print you would approve my judgment. My question was to the Minister of Resources and Development, and was based on a telegram I received yesterday morning from Dawson city. The question is, has the government decided to move the seat of government for the new territorial council from Dawson to Whitehorse, and if so, is that being done in consultation with the Yukon territorial council?

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert H. Winters (Minister of Resources and Development):
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO DECISION TO MOVE SEAT OF GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the population of Whitehorse has been increasing steadily for some years. It is now a much larger centre than Dawson city. The development of Whitehorse, together with its geographic location, have made it the centre of economic activity and communications for the territory. Although the population of Dawson city is now not large, historic interest and tradition still make it an important tourist attraction. Moreover, it is the centre of an active gold mining industry. However, the greater development in the southern part of the territory made it inevitable that consideration should be given to establishing the seat of government in Whitehorse.
This matter has been under consideration and discussion with the commissioner of the Yukon territory for some time, and it has now been decided that the change should be made in order to enable the territorial government to give more efficient and expeditious administration of the affairs of the territory.

I trust that today will be recognized as turr day in this house. To mark that day I have taken the liberty of having distributed to hon. members copies of a recent book on Newfoundland issued by the tourist development office. I believe all hon. members have received a copy of this little booklet. I might say that the booklet was compiled by Mr. Ewart Young, publisher of the Atlantic Guardian, of Montreal, in collaboration with Miss Margaret F. Godden, of the Newfoundland tourist development office. I believe those hon. members who have read it-or rather, who have looked at it, because it is chiefly made up of pictures-will recognize real merit when they see it.
In submitting this resolution I wish hon. members to know that this is a serious matter indeed and one of the greatest importance to the province of Newfoundland. Some hon. members have been joking with me about it. To hon. members who have been doing so, and whose only interest in birds apparently is in those that fly on one wing, I may say that I have no interest in such birds, at least at the present time. But to hon. members who are interested in and inclined to discuss the propensities of these peculiar one-winged birds, I may say that I am prepared, after the Easter recess, in my office or in any other suitable place they may choose, to discuss the matter in full measure with them. But until that time I have declared a closed season on discussing such peculiar birds.
This resolution, I say, deals with a serious matter. In order that hon. members may understand the problem, I will attempt to explain it to them. The legislation dealing with the subject is the Migratory Birds Convention Act of 1917, which appears as chapter 130 of the revised statutes of 1927. The original act was passed to ratify a convention made between Canada and the United States on August 16, 1916. The United States ratified the convention in 1918. By article IX of the convention it is provided that the convention shall take effect when ratified by both countries. Upon ratification the convention was to remain in effect for fifteen years from the date of ratification; and if neither party to the convention gave notice within twelve months of its intention to terminate the operation of the convention, it was to continue to remain in force for one year, and so on from year to year.
The original period of fifteen years expired in 1933 without notice of termination having been given by either party. Consequently the present position is that the convention remains in force from year to year until,

I presume, twelve-months' notice is given by either party of the desire to terminate it. By the convention certain birds described therein are enumerated under three categories: migratory game birds, migratory insectivorous birds, and other migratory non-game birds. The seasons in which such birds can be hunted are detailed. These details are set forth at pages 2768 and 2769 of volume III of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1927.
In order that hon. members may be able to understand the description of these birds, as stated in the convention, as compared with the birds named in the resolution, may I say that the description in the resolution is the form in which we know them in Newfoundland. Hown is known by the wildlife division of the Department of Resources and Development as old-squaw duck. Sea-duck is known as eider duck; divers as scoter duck and shell-birds as merganser duck.
These four forms of duck are described in subparagraph (a) of paragraph 1 of article 1 of the convention under the generic term name of wild duck, and are stated to be in the category of migratory game birds. The remaining three varieties of sea birds named in this resolution, namely, turrs, ticklaces and steams, are described in the case of turrs as murres, steams as terns and ticklaces as kitti-wake gulls. These names are the same as the names in the convention, with the exception of ticklace, which is described as a gull, and which is known to the wildlife division as the kittiwake gull. These are classed, as migratory non-game birds, and there is no open season for them at any time in the territories of the United States or of Canada.
Of these three varieties, by far the most important to the people of Newfoundland is the turr, and it is chiefly in connection with the permission to take and kill for food this bird that I am asking the consideration of the house today. It is not the purpose of the resolution to give the right to sell with respect to the other birds which I have mentioned, and which are included in the resolution namely, hown, sea-duck, diver and shell-bird. Certain seasons are proclaimed yearly in which they may be taken. This year the seasons have been set forth, and, Mr. Speaker, with the consent of the house I should like to put the table on Hansard rather than read it, as it is fairly extensive.

This statement is dated
November 8, 1949, signed by Leslie M. Tuck, dominion wildlife officer, Newfoundland, and reads as follows:
Following the union of Newfoundland and Canada, the migratory birds treaty, which was adopted by Canada and the United States more than thirty years ago, came into effect in this province. This outstanding conservation treaty was approved by the governments of the individual provinces, as well as by the dominion government, and the application of its provisions is a matter of close dominion-provincial understanding. The original concept was to provide similar and adequate conservation of valuable migratory birds throughout North America, as the best means of protecting birds that annually migrate across international boundaries. It is widely accepted as the greatest single act of wildlife conservation ever inaugurated, and is implemented throughout Canada by the Migratory Birds Convention Act.
This legislation recognizes that the protection of migratory birds is an international question, as well as a local one. It is only by international agreement under federal auspices that we can be assured that protection equivalent to that extended in one country will be given migrant birds by other countries that they annually visit. Under this agreement, certain sea birds, and all the shorebirds except two species, are absolutely protected throughout the year in all parts of Canada^ and the United States. The shooting season for migratory game birds is definitely limited in each locality, and all spring shooting is prohibited. A secondary effect, but one of the greatest importance to the species

concerned, has been the stopping of the sale of migrant game birds throughout the United States and the provinces of Canada.
The open seasons for ducks, geese and Wilson's snipe are set each year by agreement between the dominion and provincial authorities after full discussion of the conditions relating to the subject. In Newfoundland this year the open seasons for these birds began on various dates, but all terminated on October 31, except that the open season for the various kinds of eider ducks and scoter ducks will continue, throughout the coastal waters of the province, until November 30.
It is recognized that many people around the coasts of Newfoundland are accustomed to depend on the meat of the murre, or turr, as it is locally called, for food, and have made no substitute provision for the winter. Hardship might be experienced by these families if those birds could not be obtained. While the migratory birds treaty does not provide an open season for the turr, since it is not one of the game birds, the authorities do not for the present propose to interfere with residents of Newfoundland who, because of need, take and possess turrs for their own use and that of their families. This does not, however, apply to bull-birds, ticklaces, noddies or bawks, which the treaty protects throughout the year.
The sale of wild birds, because of the unnecessary and excessive destruction to which it leads, has become widely outlawed. Consequently, the sale of migratory birds is generally prohibited in the island of Newfoundland and its adjacent islands, as in other provinces and in the United States. However, as a special concession scoter and eider ducks may be sold in Newfoundland during the open season for these birds, which is from October 1 to November 30 in the Avalon peninsula and September 15 to November 30 in the remainder of the island.
There are two species of eider ducks in Newfoundland during the above mentioned season. The male of the common eider duck is a distinctive bird with a black belly, a white back and a black crown. The female is brown, as are the females of both eiders and scoters. The other species of eider is the king eider, or king bird, as it is called in some localities. The male of this species has its foreparts white and its hind1 parts black. On the water it looks something like a saddle-back gull. A further means of identification of the king eider is the large orange shield on its forehead. Its female is a brown duck similar to the female of the common eider.
There are three scoter ducks found in these waters. The scoters are the large, chunky, blackish ducks, commonly seen flying low over the waves. The white-winged scoter, sometimes called the white-winged diver, is the largest of the three, and is easily identified by its white wing patch. The surf scoter (bottle-nosed diver or skunk head) is all black except for one or two white patches on its head. The American scoter (black-winged diver) is the only duck with entirely black plumage. This and the bright orange base of the bill are good identification marks.

because I wish to see if I have the time. This petition was sent to the premier of Newfoundland who said, replying in a letter to the petitioners:
I must explain that in this matter of shooting seabirds the government of Newfoundland has no more power or authority than the government of Korea.
He said that the matter comes entirely under the control of the dominion government at Ottawa. It was the premier's understanding, that Canada, the United States

Migratory Birds Convention Act and Mexico had made a treaty in connection with the shooting of these birds, and that no provincial government or state government in the United States has any authority whatsoever in the matter. I do not know how the premier got Mexico into the treaty business, because Mexico is not concerned, so far as the treaty is concerned. Then the premier added in his letter:
It is news to me that anything has been done in this matter in White bay, or in fact, in any part of Newfoundland.
He means, in other words, that it was news to him that the people of White bay were allowed to shoot birds in this present year. That is an extraordinary statement, to my mind, because if Dr. Harrison Lewis is correct-and I have every reason to believe he is-then the premier was fully aware of what had been done, and was fully aware of the fact that in one-half the island prohibition is strictly enforced while in the other half it does not apply at the present time. He should have been aware of it, anyway- whether he was or not. Whatever knowledge he had or did not have, his departmental officials certainly had it.
I would add in that connection that whatever knowledge the departmental officials of the Newfoundland government had prior to confederation of the fact that Newfoundlanders would not be allowed to shoot these sea birds, as they had had a right to do for four hundred years, it was not known to the people of Newfoundland prior to the referendum which dealt with confederation with Canada. I venture to say that if that fact had been known, not only is it my opinion but it is the considered opinion of many people including-and I do not think I am taking chances when I say this-the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo who is now in his seat, that confederation would not have had the majority it did have. In fact, we would not be here today if the people were not allowed to shoot turrs-and hon. members from Newfoundland know it. As I say, I have received letters from all over Newfoundland in this connection, but to further buttress my argument on this point I should like to quote from a resolution which I am told was adopted unanimously at the national convention of the Young Liberal Federation of Canada meeting in Montreal on October 12, 13 and 14, 1949. This reads:
Whereas there are many people in Newfoundland particularly in the north and south areas depending entirely for their supply of fresh meat on the numerous sea birds which frequent our shores, and whereas at present the federal laws have forbidden the shooting of these birds, be it resolved that the

federal authorities take immediate steps to amend the present act to allow the people to take these birds for local consumption.
That should have some effect upon the minister. I may say that I have been informed in conversation with the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo (Mr. Carter) that following the special session last year he made a tour of his riding last fall, during which he received numerous written representations asking that the restrictions be removed. He received many petitions asking for the removal of the present restrictions. I understand from the hon. member that it is his contention that the turrs or murres which are hunted in his riding are the species known as the Brunnich's murres, as distinct from the Atlantic murres. The murres breed in Greenland during the summer months and migrate to the waters off the south and north coasts of Newfoundland during the winter months from November to March inclusive. It is the hon. member's belief that there is no proof whatever that this species ever migrates as far south as the coastal waters of the United States. The species which migrates south, the hon. member tells me, is the Atlantic species. It is said that less than one per cent of that species approach the international boundary between Canada and the United States and very few, if any, cross it.
From my discussion with the hon. member I understand that it is his belief that Newfoundlanders have been shooting these birds ever since the days of the first settlers. They have come to rely upon them as a source of food supply, particularly in the winter months when other foods are impossible to obtain, because of the lack of roads and other means of communication. As a result of lack of communication in winter these people cannot visit the larger supply firms and they must obtain their food from every possible source at hand.
The hon. member tells me that in most of his riding it is impossible to purchase fresh fruit or garden produce at any time, and this is especially so in the winter months. The little that is grown locally in his riding in the gardens is consumed long before December. Therefore the food available during the winter is deficient in vitamins and for this reason it is submitted that these birds should be allowed to be taken for food, not only to offset deficiency in vitamins but to provide a welcome variation in the staple diet of salt meat and salt fish.
The hon. member tells me that besides providing food these birds provide bait for codfish. During the winter it is too risky

for the fishermen to leave their herring nets out overnight, the herring being used as bait, and the entrails of these birds provide a very-efficient substitute. Many of the fishermen in the hon. member's riding are able to keep their boats in operation all winter as they can launch them quite easily and as a result many quintals of fish are caught with this kind of bait. Consequently the prohibition against the killing of these birds works a double hardship on a great many residents in his riding, first, by depriving them of essential food supplies and, second, by depriving them of the opportunity of obtaining bait and thereby reducing their production and their income.
As hon. members are aware, we are faced with a great problem in Newfoundland because of the incidence of tuberculosis. I have been the president of the Newfoundland Tuberculosis Association since its inception in 1945 and I am fairly familiar with the fact. My belief is that proper diet is of the greatest importance in the prevention of tuberculosis. That is not only my opinion; it has the endorsation of that well known authority, Dr. G. J. Wherrett, secretary of the Canadian Tuberculosis Association. He has given me his permission to quote him as saying that "fresh foods and vitamins are necessary for a proper diet, and proper diet has a definite relationship to the incidence of tuberculosis."
As proof of the gravity of the tuberculosis problem in Newfoundland I might point out that the death rate is 82 per 100,000 of population as compared with 30 per 100,000 in the rest of Canada, with a slightly lower figure in the United States. While this figure appears to be high, it is much lower than it was before our economic conditions improved during the last war as a result of the tremendous expenditures made by the United States in connection with the construction of bases as well as expenditures by Canada and Great Britain.
I also must give credit to our department of public health under the very able direction of Dr. L. A. Miller, assisted by Dr. J. M. McGrath, for this reduction. I feel justified in saying, moreover, that very valuable work has been done by the Newfoundland Tuberculosis Association as well, under the enthusiastic and capable leadership of our executive secretary, Mr. Walter Davis.
In line with the general contention that a proper diet is essential in waging the battle against the white plague, it is necessary that the people of Newfoundland be permitted to take these birds for food and not for sale. It is my understanding that the majority of turrs killed along the southern coast of Newfoundland are killed outside the three
Migratory Birds Convention Act mile territorial limit. I am told also that the birds closer in are in poor condition because they are partly covered with oil discharged from diesel operated vessels. Therefore they are not considered fit for eating when in that condition.
Under the present law it is permissible to kill these birds outside the three mile limit, but it is not permissible to bring them ashore. That means that if a man living on the south coast of Newfoundland wants to give his family a meal of these birds he must put the family in his boat, take them out past the three mile limit, kill the birds out there, cook the birds out there, and then wait for the food to digest. Technically speaking if they are brought in in the stomachs of his family he would be strictly guilty of a breach of the law.
Section 3 of article II of the convention permits Eskimos and Indians to take sea birds, which would include turrs. They are also permitted to take their eggs but they are not permitted to sell them. We have the ridiculous position of the Indian and Eskimo of Labrador being allowed to take these birds whereas the local Newfoundlander is not allowed to do so.

He informed me: "The terms of the treaty will apply no matter how numerous the birds may become." Further Dr. Lewis informed me that during the past thirty years hunting has not decreased the number of birds in Newfoundland and he had no knowledge of the position previous to that. His contention is that the reason the birds have not decreased in number is that the people of United States and Canada have not been shooting them. To me that is just shooting a lot of bull, but there it is. I ask how many members from the maritimes have shot and eaten any of these birds in their lifetime. Some hon. members outside the chamber have asked me why I am making such a fuss about this, why we do not just go ahead and shoot them anyhow. The answer, so that hon. members may understand, is that outside St. John's the policing of the island is done by that splendid force, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police; and under the provisions of this act they are ex officio game officers. Even if they disregarded their oath, which is unlikely, under section 8 of this act they would be liable to a fine of up to $500 or to six months' imprisonment "for conniving at breaking the law" if they did close their eyes to it. Anyone breaking the law by shooting such birds is liable to a penalty of up to $300 or six months' imprisonment or both fine and imprisonment, while subsection 2 of section 12 provides that a prosecutor who is not a game officer shall be entitled to one-half the penalty imposed. There are always informers, so there is no possibility that you could get away with shooting these birds without having someone tell on you. Certainly the mounted police are not going to take chances like that.
Another argument advanced by Dr. Lewis was that while it was difficult for people to change their habits, Newfoundland was in the position where it was necessary. My answer to that is in the words of Samuel Johnson, who said, "The chains of habit are too weak to be felt until they are too strong to be broken". The chains of Newfoundland's habits in this respect have been forged over a period of four and a half centuries.
The minister's idea is to have the dominion wildlife officer for Newfoundland co-operate with the agricultural authorities to develop the production of meat for local consumption

in and near the more remote localities of the province. To this my answer is that the theory is excellent, but I challenge him to carry it out. Cows or any other edible beasts cannot feed on rocks, and along many parts of the coastline of Newfoundland that is all there is. Moreover I understand the minister's attitude is that while he would like the convention amended for the purpose of permitting Newfoundlanders to take these birds for their own consumption, he is unable to do so because of the necessity of securing United States consent. My reply is that when the United States wished to establish bases in Newfoundland we did not ask any payment; and it is well to remember that the bases in Newfoundland were no part of the destroyers-for-bases deal. We gave up sovereignty over those portions of our country at that time freely, without any consideration whatsoever, and I think it would be a very small quid pro quo now to ask the United States government to give Newfoundlanders the right to shoot these turrs in seasons, which will be limited under the game regulations. When the bases were set up in Newfoundland we had to go through a great deal of disturbance. Our people were moved out of localities where they and their parents before them had made their homes. Their family lives were disrupted, their homes were torn down, and all the sentimental attachments that go with a home were destroyed forever in many cases. So we feel we are asking very little and that this would be very small compensation indeed for what we have had to put up with. There is no suggestion on my part of any ill will toward the Americans. We are very happy to have them there. They have brought a lot of good money and a lot of good will with them, and the relationships are pleasant indeed. But certainly there is no reason why we should not ask this small concession on their part.

Mr. Speaker, as this is my first address from the floor of this historic chamber, I should like my first words to be words of thanks to the people who sent me here. With your permission, sir, before proceeding to discuss the resolution before the house, 1 should like to express my heartfelt gratitude to my constituents for the confidence they have placed in me, and for the honour they have bestowed upon me in selecting me to represent them in this national parliament.
The subject matter of the resolution introduced by the member for St. John's East (Mr. Higgins) is one of great concern to all my constituents. I would be failing in my duty to them if I did not present their wishes here today. The numerous petitions and telegrams which I have received from all parts of my riding make it quite plain that my constituents want me to support this resolution. Although several species of sea birds are mentioned in this resolution, the importance of one species known scientifically as the murre, and locally as the turr, overshadows the importance of all the others. All the telegrams and petitions which I have received refer only to this one species, the turr. The economic value of this bird has already been pointed out by my friend the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. Higgins), as well as its importance as a factor in the health and nutrition of our people. To understand this it is necessary to know the isolated conditions under which so many of our people live.	[DOT]
In my own riding of Burin-Burgeo there are 260 settlements, of which only 33 have a population of over 300. Of those 260 settlements only about 45 are connected by roads, and 73 are connected by the Canadian National Railway coastal service. This leaves about 150 settlements without any organized system of communications whatever, either with each other or with the outside world. The only way to get from one place to another is by means of small fishing boats. In stormy weather, especially in the winter months, these settlements are completely isolated for weeks at a time.
Few communities have sufficient land for gardens or for the raising of livestock. Consequently only a tiny fraction of the food supply can be produced in the community. The nearest store is usually located in one of the larger settlements several miles away.

Because of this isolated condition which I have just described, the people are forced to supplement their food supply from natural sources. In this respect they are in much the same position as the woodsmen and the trappers. The only difference is that for our people nature provides a food supply in the form of sea birds instead of in the form of land birds and small animals. Our fishermen have been dependent upon this source of food from the time of the earliest settlers, and it came as rather a shock to them when they learned that confederation had deprived them of this right which they had exercised for so many years.
Their first reaction was that something had been put over on them; because it is logical to assume that the application of federal game laws would be taken up by the departments concerned when the terms of union were under discussion. Yet no mention was made of this restriction when the issue of confederation was placed before the people. Their second reaction was one of vexation and resentment at losing a right which they had enjoyed for so many years, and particularly one which affected their lives in so many ways. Resentment is always a bad thing in any form. It is a sort of cancer of the spirit which grows by feeding on itself. One of its effects is to prevent us from thinking about the question objectively.
As I understand it, my duty in this house is not only to make known the views of my people but to search for the truth and to present that truth as I see it both to my constituents and to this parliament; not only that, but also to point out the direction in which I believe the truth impels us to move. In this connection there are a few points to which I should like to direct attention. The first point is that there is available hltogether too little authentic information for us to be able to make a definite decision as to what is the right thing to do in this case.
The restriction that brought about this resolution arises out of an international treaty which affects other nations and other provinces. We do not know to what extent the numbers of these sea birds have increased during the time that the treaty has been in force. We do not know whether the rate of increase is sufficient to withstand the slaughter which might result if all the Atlantic provinces insisted on exercising their right to kill these bird's, as legally they would be able to do should the treaty be amended.
In the second place, there is some doubt in my mind at least as to whether these birds known as turrs or murres should properly be included in the terms of this international treaty at all. In my opinion, turrs are not
Migratory Birds Convention Act migratory birds. To my mind, a migratory bird is one whose natural habits, food supply and body temperature compel it to move from one country to another to seek climatic conditions essential to its natural existence and the propagation of its species. This definition certainly does not apply to the turr. Only a small percentage of these birds actually cross the international boundary, and I believe that those either drift southwards with the ocean currents or are blown southwards by the prevailing winds. These birds are not built for flying. They have relatively small wings and they can fly only a short distance at a time before coming down on the water. They are therefore different in this respect from other migratory birds. The fact that a few of them may drift or be blown across the international boundary does not, in my opinion, make them migratory birds.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to see this question settled on a basis of what is right; that sentiment applies not only to this question but to every question that comes before this house. In no other way can we effectively serve the interests of our people or of our nation. We can determine what is right only if we are guided by the moral principles involved. The first principle that comes to my mind is that democracy must concern itself with the needs of the people, or else it ceases to be democracy. The second principle is that we are our brother's keeper and we should care for each other enough to put the needs of others before our own. In this respect we must bear in mind the fact that our Indian and Eskimo brothers need these birds even worse than do our Newfoundland fishermen, because they have a total meat diet and they live on what they can catch and kill from day to day. For their sakes, therefore, these birds must not be permitted to become extinct. If that should happen, our Indians and Eskimos would suffer far greater hardship than anyone else; and for this very reason the birds must be protected. Whether total protection is necessary, however, is quite another matter. The number of birds killed by the Newfoundland fishermen is relatively small, as they do not appear in any numbers until from December to March; and at that time of the year the weather is so stormy that the fishermen can get out in their boats only about once or twice a week to kill them. Far more destruction is caused by foxes, which devour their eggs and kill the young, and also by crude oil pumped out by ships at sea, which destroys thousands of adult birds at a time. However, if some protective measures are necessary, our people will be the first to agree to a limitation of the shooting season,

Migratory Birds Convention Act and on the number of birds to be taken. But the overriding factor, as I see it, is that of human need. This principle is already recognized by the treaty, which grants exemption to the Indians and the Eskimos. I believe that this principle should be extended to our Newfoundland fishermen in those areas where a definite need exists, and to other provinces as well where the need can be established. I believe that if proposals are put forward to the countries and to the provinces concerned on this basis they will agree to an amendment.
It is because I view the resolution in this light that I give it my wholehearted support.

Mr. Speaker, first of all I should like to congratulate my colleague, the hon. member for St. John's East	(Mr.	Higgins),	on	thecomprehensive presentation of the case which he put forward here this afternoon; so much so, that he has left	little	for	anyone	whofollows him to say.	I should	like	to	congratulate him also on the strong and impassioned plea that he has put forward to the government and to the house to alter the law in relation to the birds to which we are referring. I believe	that	he	has,	by	the
extracts that he has given from representative people in Newfoundland, faithfully portrayed the feelings of a great majority of the residents around the coast of Newfoundland.
It is obvious to everyone that my colleague has gone to great pains to prepare this presentation, and I feel sure that the people concerned will be most grateful to him for the forceful manner in, which he has put their case forward.
I should also like to take this opportunity to congratulate the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo (Mr. Carter) on his maiden speech. If he approaches all the questions before this house in the same broadminded manner in which he has tackled this question, then he will deserve to receive the praise of all hon. members.
As a member, sir, of a riding which, outside the city of St. John's, has 300 miles of coastline where there are 20,000 people living in a hundred settlements, and living in houses the front doors of which face upon the ocean to show that the sea is their highway, I feel I must support my colleague from St. John's East in recommending to this house the adoption of this resolution. But I think a case should be put forward so that the proposal could be accepted on its merits, and not from any show of sympathetic consideration to the people in Newfoundland.


We are not looking for any special favours in this. I believe we have a case. While this subject is very important to thousands of people in Newfoundland, we must also recognize that there is a class of persons who have another regard for the birds, and who regard the question of preservation and conservation of birdlife as very important, too. I refer to the almost unknown group of men, naturalists and ornithologists, and here I should like to pay a tribute to that class of men who have taken, such a deep interest in the life of birds over the years, and to whom we all owe a great deal for their preservation. If we could only imagine what life on this planet would be without having birds we would realize what a debt we all owe to these men through the past centuries. Imagine spring without the robin or blackbird or thrush! Imagine summer without the swallow or the skylark, or early morning in the forests without the whistling of the birds! Imagine a ship at sea without the friendly following gulls! How much poorer the world would be without the beauty of the humming bird, the soaring eagle, or the song of the nightingale. The birds of the air play an important part in the Divine plan of creation.
To those lovers of birds, like the late Jack Miner, not only the people of Canada, but the people of the whole world, owe a great debt of gratitude, and it is surprising and even shocking to realize that just south of Jack Miner's sanctuary in southwestern Ontario at the time the birds take their flight to go south hundreds of people line up with shotguns, sportsmen, and shoot into the mass of birds darkening the sky. The naturalists and the ornithologists therefore, by their patience, by their perseverance, by their studies and their experiments, have accumulated a mass of valuable information of great benefit to mankind. They have succeeded in identifying the birds, noting their habits and portraying them even so that outside the places of their habitat we can see what they look like and learn all about them. There may be little doubt that those men have great influence on the government, and the government will act upon their advice. There is little doubt that it was largely due to their work that the birds to which we are referring today have not only not decreased in number, but have actually tended to increase in recent years. But, of course, it must be understood that even without the protection afforded these birds under the terms of the migratory birds convention it would not be possible to extinguish this class of birds. There is no danger of extinction of the turr as there was

of the great auk because they have greater mobility and there are far greater numbers of them. .
In the case of the great auk, Mr. Speaker, which became extinct nearly a hundred years ago in Newfoundland, its wings by constant use in the water had become a sort of flipper. The bird had become entirely aquatic, so that when it was being hunted it could not fly away, and therefore was shot in great numbers. In fact at times the fishermen used to put down planks from the land to the ship and drive the auks, which were very much like penguins, on board ship and take them away in that manner.
Nor is there serious danger of any great depletion in the flocks of those birds; and those who heard that letter which my colleague read this afternoon will agree that from testimony of a high character there seem to be millions upon millions of these birds. I know that on one island off Witless bay, which is a part of my riding, about 21 miles south of St. John's, there are many thousands of those birds. You can look at that island and you can see those birds lined up in ranks like troops, hundred of thousands of them. Every little ledge is covered with birds. Anyone who has seen them there would hardly think that they could be easily extinguished.
What I believe is a more serious cause of destruction of birds of that kind is the pollution of water by the oil-burning steamers.
It is the practice of many engineers on the steamers, after the tanks have been exhausted of oil, to fill them up with water; and when they are approaching port they discharge this water, so that they can refuel when they go into port. When they discharge the water large quantities of oil waste and sludge go into the sea; and since the oil is lighter than water it floats on top of the water and spreads out over great distances so that all the birds within the neighbourhood get coated with this oil. It permeates their plumage so that they cannot rise from the water, and they cannot dive for food. Therefore they become thin and die.
I believe that attempts have been made to control the deposit of oil on the surface of the water in this manner. And although many people have co-operated, there are still some who do not, and the oil from these steamers and the oil from wrecks along the coast escaping into the water kills thousands of birds every year.
The question comes to my mind as I suppose it comes to many hon. members; and my colleague dealt with it this afternoon: Why do naturalists work so hard to preserve and

Migratory Birds Convention Act propagate these species? It is hardly for the purpose of giving us pleasure. The answer which Dr. Harrison Lewis is supposed to have given my hon. friend and colleague is that it is done just to see them increase and multiply. It seems to me that is not a justification. It is not a sound reason.
These birds are like other game birds, such as partridge, plover, snipe or the brown duck, which have been created by God for the benefit of man. People who live in places where these birds congregate have the right to shoot them, in the appropriate season, just the same as sportsmen have the right to go out to shoot partridge, caribou or moose.
A wise exception was made in the convention referred to by the hon. member in respect of Eskimos and Indians, who have been accustomed to taking these birds and using the eggs as well, from time immemorial. It is appropriate to point out that at the conference which took place shortly after April 1, 1949, between the representatives of the provincial department of natural resources and the federal government officials, it was recognized as set out at page 29 of the report of the Department of Resources and Development for 1950 that "in the economy of Newfoundland migratory birds were of great importance".
As a result of that decision, for the first year the closed season was not extended to Newfoundland. This winter, however, for the first time, half of the island', beginning somewhere north of St. John's-about forty miles I believe

and extending down south along the south coast, and then north again as far as Cape St. Gregory on the west coast of Newfoundland, the southern half of the island was brought within the closed season, and fishermen along that stretch of coast are not allowed to shoot birds this year. Next year the remainder of the island will be covered by the closed season. After that the birds can multiply in their millions and laugh heartily at the fishermen.
It is this sudden change of policy which has caused surprise and consternation, and even bitterness among large numbers of people in Newfoundland. So general and so intense are the feelings of the people on this subject that it has been said by many supporters of the federal government, and supporters of confederation, that if the people had known they were not going to have the right to shoot these birds, confederation would have been defeated by a substantial majority.
Hon. members from other parts of the country, especially from inland parts, may find it hard to understand why there is so much commotion over this subject, and why people are so concerned about wild game. I

Migratory Birds Convention Act shall try to explain why. We have a coastline six thousand miles in length on which there are about twelve hundred settlements. During the winter months there is no communication at all with many of those settlements. People cannot get to the stores; no butcher comes around, and it is easy to see that in small villages, where there is very little arable land, it is impossible to raise sheep or cattle. Some people raise pigs and have what they call a barrel of pork put down for the winter. But often, they are not able to get young pigs in the spring, and the result is that they have not the pork to eat when the winter comes along. To a large extent they rely upon the supply of meat they can get from shooting birds.
People in those outports spend a great deal of time gathering firewood. Throughout the country, except in the larger centres, wood is burned. The people go into the forest and collect -the firewood-a year's supply. On suitable days they will go out to shoot turrs or duck. People in those isolated settlements are bound to take advantage of everything nature offers to keep the wolf from the door, and to live until their normal trade relations open in the spring.
It is easy to remind hon. members tnat the price of meat today is prohibitive, almost, to any ordinary workingman in a city such as Ottawa. I have heard working people in the United States as well as in Canada complain about the high prices they have to pay for fresh meat. In those isolated settlements which are so far away from the great centres of production, accordingly, the people in Newfoundland rely to a very large extent -much greater than the people in other parts of Canada-upon wild game such as rabbits, caribou, moose and wild birds.
Some may ask: Why do they -not raise poultry? I have asked myself that question. I have said, "Why do not the people have eggs and poultry?" It was pointed out to me that it is not practicable to have a poultry farm if there is no market nearby. One has to make an outlay for equipment to run the farm. He must pay for feed, which would have to be imported over long distances. Then, if there is no ready market nearby in which to sell poultry and eggs, one cannot dispose of any surplus. What are the people to do?
You will say to me, "Eat them." But there is no need for such a large quantity, with the result that they have become discouraged. They have seen large poultry farms in the vicinity of St. John's become failures, and there is very little encouragement for individuals in the isolated outports to follow that practice. I believe that through the


co-operative methods to which I have referred several times in the house, but which have not yet been practised sufficiently in Newfoundland, in time that difficulty will be overcome. In a large part of Newfoundland however individualism still rules and retards progress and development. The agitation therefore to procure the repeal of this regulation draws attention to a great problem still to be solved, namely that of enabling the people of Newfoundland to possess a sound year-round economy, outside the great industrial centres.
I can well recall my first introduction to the wild migratory non-game birds. Back in the spring of 1923 I was engaged in an election, and when we went into the village of Branch we were met with open arms-and I might add that the people who opposed us were met with open arms later. We were taken to a boarding house, and I remember well how clean and comfortable the place was. The piece de resistance was wild sea duck- and anyone who has not tasted wild sea duck or turr has a treat in store. Unless the government has this regulation rescinded, he may never have that privilege. I ask hon. members to consider the fair and reasonable proposition put forward by my hon. friend, namely that of granting to the industrious and hardy people who have worked so hard the same rights granted to Eskimos and Indians in connection with taking these birds for food.
The reason that privilege is given the Indians and Eskimos is not only that they have had it from time immemorial, but that it is a means of obtaining food. It is the natural method for them to do so. As my hon. friend from Burin-Burgeo (Mr. Carter) pointed out, the people who live along the seacoast where the birds congregate in great numbers should be granted the same rights. Such rights could be restricted to a certain period of the year-I do not think there would be any objection to that. I suggest that this would not seriously deplete the great stock of birds, and would assure to the people of Newfoundland the food necessary to help carry them over the long winter months.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the question is put I want to say that I support this resolution. I want to congratulate the mover, the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. Higgins), upon the able manner in which he has presented this resolution. As one who was born in an outport of Newfoundland and who as a youth had to depend to a large extent upon wild sea birds for fresh food, I can corroborate everything that has been said by the three hon. members

from Newfoundland with regard to the importance of these birds to the people of that province.
It is unfortunate that Newfoundlanders should have to rely to such a large extent upon these birds as a source of food. It is also unfortunate that the incidence of tuberculosis should be so high. If this debate has done one thing, I am sure that it has impressed upon every hon. member and the government the nature of the task which is before us in raising the standard of living in Newfoundland and providing its people with the opportunity to earn a livelihood and to reach a status where they will no longer be dependent upon such an uncertain source of food supply.
There are one or two things we should keep in mind in connection with the convention which is the subject of this debate. Until Newfoundland came into confederation the convention was not observed in that province as they were not a party to the convention. Newfoundlanders were free to take these birds as occasion arose. From all the evidence available this practice has had no effect upon depleting the birds.
The second fact to be kept in mind is that Newfoundland is probably the only part of any country which is a party to the convention where this matter is of such grave importance. The matter is not of significance to other parts of Canada or to the United States because these birds frequent the coast line and bays of Newfoundland.
Since there is no evidence that these birds are likely to become extinct even when taken for food, as they have been for centuries, there is no common-sense reason why this resolution should not be adopted and the Canadian government seek to make some arrangement with the other parties to the convention whereby Newfoundlanders may continue to exercise a privilege they have enjoyed for centuries.
I can see no sound reason why this particular species, which is of significance only to Newfoundland, should be protected to the point where there is no open season. Other wildlife of interest to people in all parts of Canada is protected, but the protection is limited in that there are open seasons. This particular species can serve no other purpose than to provide food, and therefore I strongly support the previous members in urging that this resolution pass.

The first thing we need to do in respect to this problem is what we should do in respect to all other problems which confront Canada. We live in a great country where varying conditions prevail. Problems which are of vital concern to one area may hardly have been heard of in other parts of the country. The result is a slight inclination on the part of many members to treat lightly the problems of areas remote from their own. We must teach each other with the utmost speed to refrain from any tendency to discount the seriousness of a problem facing another part of Canada with which we do not happen to be familiar. That is the only way in which we shall be able to make this country as mighty and as great as the Creator evidently intended it should be.
I listened with much interest to the discussion of this problem in respect of turrs. 1 must confess that three weeks ago I did not know that there were such things as turrs and at first I wondered whether they were really worth considering. The hon. member for St. John's East suggested that I give the matter more than passing thought, which I did, and I find that after all it is a serious problem and one worthy of consideration.
Therefore I do not hesitate to rise this afternoon for a few moments to express my ardent sympathy with the people of Newfoundland and to indicate my support in the attempt to solve this problem. In saying that, I think I can speak for the whole of the Social Credit group and the province of Alberta. We have plenty of problems of our own and therefore we can give the most sympathetic attention to this problem faced by our sister province. We shall be prepared to give equally sympathetic consideration to every problem that affects this [DOT] dominion from one coast to the other.
In respect of this problem of turrs, I am deeply interested in what we are going to do to find a solution. After what I have heard today and the study I have given the subject I am convinced that it is a problem which simply must be solved in the way Newfoundland wants it solved. They have a perfect right to have this concession obtained for them and granted to them, because from what has been said here the matter of turrs is evidently of vital importance to their health and economy. What we are going to do about it is the great question. It occurs to

Migratory Birds Convention Act me, Mr. Speaker, that probably three lines of attack on this problem are open. From the experience I have had with him I am sure the minister does not need any suggestion from me that it will be necessary to attack this problem with the utmost energy and resourcefulness. I am sure that he is going to do that, and his department with him. Nevertheless I am assuring him that he has my support in so doing.
It seems to me we could probably establish that the turr is not properly classified as a migratory bird. We have a migratory birds convention. The evidence I have obtained thus far and the information adduced in this discussion indicate quite strongly that without too much in the way of mental gymnastics one could establish the fact that the turr is not a migratory bird in the sense in which that expression is used in the convention. I fancy that we would find considerable sympathy for this approach to the problem in the minds of enlightened and well informed people in the United States. If they did object to classifying this bird as non-migratory, then possibly we could prevail upon the United States to look at this matter from the angle that when Newfoundland entered confederation she was not aware that in doing so she would be depriving her people of the privilege of shooting turrs, and because of that fact special consideration ought to be given that province. When we bear in mind that for generations Newfoundland was a self-governing sister dominion in the British commonwealth, I think consideration ought to be given that approach and a special allowance made in the case of that province. This line of attack might be successful.
If the United States authorities were not prepared to grant the validity of those two arguments, however, it seems to me they should be prepared to grant concessions on the following ground. Here is a bird which enters vitally not only into the sporting life of Newfoundland as a migratory bird under the convention, but which enters into the very economy of the province. In the first place it constitutes an important food during considerable periods of the year over a wide area of Newfoundland; in the second place it is useful and necessary as bait for codfish.
If none of these three arguments taken separately should be sufficient, I would certainly think the three arguments taken together ought to constitute arguments that would carry sufficient weight with the United States authorities to cause them to grant us the privilege of making the exception in the case of Newfoundland, which obviously the situation requires.


With these three suggestions as to possible methods of approaching the matter I shall conclude, merely observing once more that Newfoundlanders can count on the Social Crediters of Alberta, anyway, being right behind them in all their efforts to obtain the rights they believe they should enjoy.

Mr. Speaker, in supporting what has been placed before this house so clearly and in such forceful terms by the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. Higgins) I wish to refer to some aspects of this discussion relating more to the legal phases of the problem than to the questions involved in consideration of the birdlife itself. While I cannot claim that direct association which has been put forward by the hon. member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy), at least I can claim with some pride to be one of those in this house with very direct family associations with Newfoundland.
The subject has been well placed before hon. members, and the importance of the birds mentioned in this resolution has been sufficiently emphasized so there is no necessity of repeating to hon. members the arguments in favour of consideration being given this resolution and an appropriate amendment of the act itself, which of course would involve discussion with the government of the United States. One point that has emerged from some of the correspondence that has been exchanged in regard to this subject is the suggestion that there are difficulties in the way of making exceptions in a particular case. I submit there is no practical difficulty in the way of appropriate amendments to the act following discussion with the proper authorities representing the United States government. The Migratory Birds Convention Act, which is chapter 130 of the revised statutes of Canada, 1927, makes it clear that there can be exceptions. It makes it clear that those exceptions need not be general, relating to the whole of Canada, but that they may be specific exceptions made in relation to a single province. That is shown by the various exceptions in the act itself, as well as in the appendices to the act. I would point out that in addition to the exceptions already mentioned by those who have spoken there is a group of exceptions starting with section 20 of the regulations which relate not to birdlife itself but which indicate that the provisions of this act be made to apply to different provinces of Canada in different ways. Section 20 reads:
In the province of Newfoundland, no person shall hunt, kill, or attempt to kill a migratory game bird by the use of an automatic firearm, including a firearm loaded by recoil or "auto-loading."

I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the very fact that there is a separate exception in regard to the firearms to be used in connection with the birds covered by this convention and the statute itself indicates that any provision of the act which is regarded as desirable and appropriate could be used, after steps have been taken which should be taken to produce that result. The sections immediately following this deal with exceptions in other provinces in Canada in connection with the use of firearms.
Then section 30 is an exception in relation to the birds themselves, and that is under the heading "Permits for Scientific Purposes." Section 30 provides that special permits may be given to kill, hunt, capture injure, take, molest, buy, sell, ship, transport or possess migratory birds or their eggs or nests for any scientific purpose. The section then goes on to explain how those permits shall be issued and to whom. I mentioned section 30 because the very fact that there can be an exception for scientific purposes demonstrates beyond all argument that there could equally be an exception for the purpose envisaged by this motion, namely the provision of necessary food to those parts of Newfoundland which have been accustomed to this particular food.
As I pointed out, the very fact that a number of exceptions are made to apply to particular provinces indicates that such a provision could relate to Newfoundland alone, or to any part of Newfoundland, without violating the general intent or purpose of this act. Following the act itself there are a series of schedules, and those schedules differ for each of the different provinces of Canada. Those schedules cover the open seasons for different kinds of birds, including some of the birds covered by this resolution. There again we see clearly demonstrated that there is an established practice for dealing with this subject in relation to the particular problem which each province presents.
There is also evidence contained in those schedules that the government has indicated its willingness to deal with the various aspects of this problem in relation to limited areas in separate provinces. The act itself makes it clear, therefore, that if the government is convinced that there should be an exception in the interests of the people of Newfoundland, there is nothing to prevent that exception being made.
In examining this subject, and considering what the United States would be likely to do if proper and sufficiently vigorous representations were made by the Canadian government concerning the subject, it is important to look at the convention under which both the Canadian and United States

The point really was this. The leader of the opposition indicated that the law shows that exceptions can be made. It is not the law that shows that exceptions can be made. That is a matter of treaty. The treaty makes it quite clear that exceptions, such as those the hon. gentleman mentioned, can be made. The treaty makes that clear. The treaty likewise makes it clear that with regard to these birds, which are called murres in the treaty and which are apparently called turrs locally, the prohibition of shooting or otherwise killing is absolute. So that actually to draw an inference from the Canadian law that a change can be effected is to draw a wrong inference. But of course no person will dispute the fact that it is always possible to open up discussions with a foreign country.
With respect to the whole question of the problem of the Newfoundlanders, there is no one but who must approach and view it with the greatest of sympathy. Here are people, we learn now, who have been using these birds for food for an exceedingly long time. It has been said even that this has been going on for four hundred years. By reason of confederation with Canada they find that there is first of all a danger that this food will be taken away from them. Later on one part of the island finds that indeed the opportunity of continuing to shoot these birds has been taken away from them. The other part of the island is facing the commencement of enforcement of the law there also. No person can help being sympathetic to the problem of the islanders, when he locks at a matter like that fairly in the face.
I have been aware of the difficulties for some little time. Before I became parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Resources and Development, various members from Newfoundland had come and talked the matter over with me, and had written to me at great length about it. They thought that I might have some knowledge of it dating from the time when I was in the department of mines and resources. I speak of them usually by name, not remembering their constituencies; but the hon. member for Trinity-Conception (Mr. Stick), the hon. member for Grand Falls-White Bay (Mr. MARCH 14, 1951
Ashbourne), the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo (Mr. Carter) and the hon. member for Humber-St. George's (Mr. Kent) all have written to me at great length, and have argued with me in the corridors and in my room. Whenever I met any of my colleagues from Newfoundland I thought it was almost certain that the subject of discussion would be turrs. I have had turrs, vicariously as it were, for breakfast, lunch and dinner nearly every day.
Then of course more recently the department has had representation from a number of places in Newfoundland. I have marked some of them down here. As my notes show it, petitions have come in from Grand Bank, Port die Grave, Hermitage, Sagona Island, Fortune Bay, Red Island, Placentia Bay, Little Paradise and a number of other places. There is no doubt about it that every person who has given any consideration at all to the matter has approached it in a most sympathetic way and that every person is desirous of finding some way of restoring to the Newfoundlanders the privilege they had had for so long or of working out something that will be a little bit less unpleasantly drastic than what we have had presented to us here today.
There is something about the treaty itself that might be kept in mind. I understand that we were engaged for a long time in the negotiations that led up to the signing of this treaty. A great many people in the United States and a great many people in Canada for many years were striving to get some treaty of this sort to protect birds that live sometimes on one side of the line and sometimes on the other. Eventually they succeeded. It was in 1916 that the treaty was signed. Sir Robert Borden was prime minister at that time, and I understand that he himself took a great interest in this treaty. That is what I have been told by some of the old-timers around here. There have not been any changes in the treaty since that time. There have not been any changes in the law except perhaps some few regulation changes in order better to carry out the obligations that we had under the treaty. I may say that at the time that Sir Robert Borden's government was able to effect this treaty it was received with acclaim in all parts of the house. Sir Wilfrid Laurier spoke at some length in favour of it at the time, and complimented the government of the day on its achievement. Bird lovers, sportsmen and many other types of people were greatly pleased at the time. There is, however, something that I think has been mentioned here this afternoon-and it will do no harm to repeat it-that should be kept in mind with reference to this treaty. It
Migratory Birds Convention Act appeals to me, at any rate. When this treaty was negotiated in 1916 it was for Canada as it then existed, and for the United States as it then existed. Neither of the contracting parties had in contemplation at all the island of Newfoundland, or any of the birds which swim or float around there. When one says that, the inclination develops in his mind that the United States might view with favour the proposal that Newfoundland should not be deprived of turrs, or the treaty should not apply, to some extent at any rate, to Newfoundland, since in the bargain they did not have Newfoundland in mind. Having spoken of the possibility of amending the treaty, I do think a person ought to give us some warning with respect to it. Every person is familiar with attempts that have been made to change a law. At times some little almost inconsequential change is desired in some statute. And what do we find? Well, we find that when that is pressed a great many other changes are suggested, and after they all pile up those who have had the idea of changing the statute change their minds and say, I think we had better not open up the statute at all. Every person in the house must, I feel sure, have experienced that sort of thing.
The same sort of thing is a danger with regard to a treaty. I have not made any treaties, nor revised any treaties; but common sense teaches any person that when you go to a contracting party to an agreement of this sort you may be met with quite a number of proposals by the other contracting party which in effect he would be offering as a quid pro quo to his agreement to do that which you are asking him to do. All the people of the New England states, and in fact all of the people of all of the states, would have the right to come forward and make proposals in case we attempt to open this treaty. Likewise, numbers of the other provinces are interested, and we might expect the same sort of thing there; consequently, it does seem to me that in any attempt to open up the treaty we should proceed most cautiously and before we actually ask for something find out, if we can, what the answer would be. Whether there would be any counter-proposals, whether if there were any counter-proposals we would like them or dislike them, because we wish to make sure in any discussion about the revision of this treaty that our second condition would not be worse than the first. I think that concludes what I wish to say on the resolution, with the exception of some comments I would make concerning some pencilled notes I have before me. I shall deal with what they bring to mind.
The leader of the opposition spoke about these birds becoming extinct. My information from ornithologists is that they are a slow-producing bird. Apparently the pair, male and female, produce only one chick a year, and this means perhaps only five or six in a lifetime.
Birds of this kind are confronted with many hazards, in addition to that offered by the gun. One hon. member suggested that Scotch engineers on liners kill a great many of them with oil. It would seem therefore that they are certainly not a type of bird which increases quickly. I do not say this to the

house with any authority, because I am not an ornithologist. However, since the matter has been discussed it has come to my mind that ornithologists have told me what I am now stating.
There has also been some question as to whether these birds are migratory or not. I think it was the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) who suggested that they are not, that therefore the law should not apply to them, and that the treaty did not apply.
The difficulty is that in the treaty they are mentioned by name. Whether they are migratory or not, in fact, does not matter, because the name is mentioned. However, if indeed it can be shown that these are not true migratory birds, then of course there would be a good opportunity for having them removed from the treaty in any negotiation which might be started.
I return to what I said at the outset. I believe every person who considers this matter at all, quite aside from what was expressed so eloquently by various members who supported the resolution, must view this problem with a great deal of sympathy for the people involved. Let me assure Canadians from Newfoundland that every other kind of Canadian with whom I have spoken has that attitude in mind toward the problem.
The only question is one of practicality. If it turns out to be practical to bring relief, then I feel sure the people of Newfoundland may expect it. If it is not practical, then I feel sure they are the kind of people who will accept the fact of impracticability.

Mr. Speaker,
perhaps I should say a few words on the resolution because of the fact that the administration of the Migratory Birds Convention Act comes within the Department of Resources and Development.
As was said previously, this question has been considered for some time. A few months ago the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo (Mr. Carter) spoke to me and wrote me a letter in which he told me of the dire distress of some of the people of Newfoundland because they were now unable to shoot turrs, since entering confederation. The hon. member for Trinity-Conception (Mr. Stick) also spoke to me, as have others. Then the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. Higgins) placed his resolution on the order paper, following which we had a number of discussions which were helpful to me, and I hope they were helpful to him.
14, 1951	1259
Migratory Birds Convention Act
His position was that he wanted to know the attitude of the department with respect to the administration of the act and the convention. We arranged for Dr. Lewis, who is most directly concerned with the administration, to spend some time with the hon. member. The results of the conversation they had have been made known in the chamber today. We have enjoyed the dissertation of the hon. member for St. John's East just as we have that of the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Browne). I think all hon. members who have spoken, from both sides of the house, have added to our knowledge of the problem facing the people of Newfoundland and especially the hardships they undergo in the wintertime when their normal sources of food are not available to them. I believe certain light has been shed on the subject which will be helpful to the people of Newfoundland in understanding the position of the federal government in the [DOT] matter.
When the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) spoke it seemed to me that he grouped all these birds together as migratory game birds, and implied that there was an open season on all of them. The fact of the matter is that in article I of the migratory birds treaty there are three general classifications, the first of which is migratory game birds; the second, migratory insectivorous birds; and the third, other migratory non-game birds.
The murre or turr is one of those birds classified as a migratory non-game bird, and therefore not eligible for shooting at any season of the year. There are however a number of other birds under the act and on which there is an open season. These birds can be shot by the people of Newfoundland and elsewhere in the seasons prescribed.
Perhaps it might be helpful if I were to mention again the names of the birds set out in the resolution standing in the name of the hon. member for St. John's East, and place on record the names by which they are commonly known in Newfoundland, and by which they are known ordinarily elsewhere. For example, there is the hown which, in Newfoundland, is known as the hown, but which is known elsewhere as the old squaw duck. In Burin and the Burin peninsula the open season is December 5 to February 28, and for the remainder of Newfoundland from December 5 to December 28; in Labrador it is from October 2 to December 26.
